# Introduction

Forest research teams often have several sources of environmental information for the same plot. Elevation may come from a ground survey or a digital elevation model. Soil measurements may be stored as a table of sampling locations, while canopy height or disturbance intensity may arrive as raster files. These sources can describe different years, spatial resolutions and areas of coverage. This tutorial shows how to put those sources into a common spatial frame. It also shows how to extract environmental information at different scales:

-   specific points, e.g. tree locations;
-   buffers around specific points;
-   quadrats;
-   polygons of arbitrary shape.

These targets support different ecological questions: soil conditions at individual trees can help explain growth or mortality; buffers describe the surrounding environment; quadrats support abundance or composition analyses at different spatial scales; and irregular polygons can represent canopy gaps or treatment areas.

The familiar CTFS/fgeo approach returned elevation, slope and convexity for a regular quadrat grid, commonly 20 × 20 m. Here, preparing environmental layers and choosing extraction targets are separate steps. The same layers can therefore serve several analyses, alongside independently supplied soil or canopy data. A pseudo-legacy example below returns to quadrat-level topography for users who need that familiar output.

# Data and setup

## Example data

The example data used here combines real elevation and soil data for the 50-ha Barro Colorado Island (BCI) plot in Panama. Terrain layers come from the `derive_topography()` workflow applied to elevational data. Soil layers are prepared independently. Native raster grids are retained for extraction, and an additional example shows how to create a common grid when an analysis needs one. Habitat classification and categorical extraction are covered separately. All inputs are in `data_examples/` at the repository root. See its [dataset notes](../../data_examples/README.md) for provenance.

-   **`census1.txt`** and **`census2.txt`** contain the first two BCI tree censuses, nominally 1982 and 1985. They are historical census exports already included in fgeo2. Census 1 measurements span 1981--1983. Credit goes to the BCI census team, including Stephen P. Hubbell, Robin B. Foster, Richard Condit and collaborators, and Smithsonian/ForestGEO.
-   **`bci-elevation.csv`** contains 20,301 elevation grid locations, with columns `x`, `y` and `z` in metres. Its numerical contents match `BCIelev.tsv` in the Condit et al. archive, released under CC0. Positions run from 0 to 1,000 m in x and 0 to 500 m in y, at 5 m intervals. These are input grid locations, rather than raster-cell boundaries.
-   **`bci-soils-wolf-2015.csv`** is the complete soil dataset of Wolf et al. (2015), [Geospatial observations on tropical forest surface soil chemistry](https://doi.org/10.1890/15-0558.1). It includes 625 sampled locations, all soil variables and both local and UTM coordinates. The [publisher's dataset deposit](https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.3562863) is CC0. P and Ca illustrate the main workflow, while all measurements remain available for other analyses.

## Locate project

Run the following code from the repository root or this tutorial's folder. When working elsewhere, replace `path.to.fgeo2` with the full path to your local repository. Output files go to a temporary folder by default.

```{r}
#| label: setup-environment
#| results: hide
#| message: false

# install.packages(c("terra", "sf", "interp", "exactextractr"))
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(exactextractr)

path.to.fgeo2 = if(file.exists("../../fgeo2.Rproj")) "../.." else "."
# path.to.fgeo2 = "/full/path/to/fgeo2"
input.dir = file.path(path.to.fgeo2, "data_examples")
output.dir = file.path(tempdir(), "fgeo2-environment")
dir.create(output.dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

source(file.path(path.to.fgeo2, "06_topography_habitat/R/new/topography-variables.R"))
source(file.path(path.to.fgeo2, "03_spatial/R/new/quadrats.R"))

# Shared options. Interpolation choices are described below.
plot.extent = c(0, 1000, 0, 500)  # xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax
terrain.resolution = 5
soil.resolution = 20
buffer.radius = 15
set.seed(123)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5)
```

## Load census records and stable identifiers

Read tags and identifiers as character strings, preserving leading zeros. The stem identifier is unique within each supplied census. A combined census--stem key distinguishes repeated observations of the same stem. Several stems can belong to one tree.

```{r}
#| label: load-censuses

id.columns <- c(TreeID = "character",
                StemID = "character",
                Tag = "character",
                StemTag = "character",
                Quadrat = "character")

census1 <- read.delim(file.path(input.dir, "census1.txt"),
                      colClasses = id.columns, check.names = FALSE)

census2 <- read.delim(file.path(input.dir, "census2.txt"),
                      colClasses = id.columns, check.names = FALSE)

trees <- rbind(census1, census2)
trees$point_id <- paste(trees$Census, trees$StemID, sep = "_")
stopifnot(!anyNA(trees$point_id), !anyDuplicated(trees$point_id))

```

## Load elevation and soil tables

Keep the complete input tables. Variable selection takes place when preparing layers for a particular analysis. The original soil file contains a space before the `utm_n` column name, which is removed on import here. Its [metadata](https://esapubs.org/archive/ecol/E096/204/metadata.php) describes methods, units, missing values and detection limits.

```{r}
#| label: load-environment

xyz <- read.csv(file.path(input.dir, "bci-elevation.csv"))
soils <- read.csv(file.path(input.dir, "bci-soils-wolf-2015.csv"),
                  check.names = FALSE)

names(soils) <- trimws(names(soils))
stopifnot(nrow(xyz) == 20301L, nrow(soils) == 625L,
          !anyDuplicated(xyz[c("x", "y")]), !anyDuplicated(soils$uid))

head(soils[c("uid", "gx", "gy", "M3P", "M3Ca")])
```

# Prepare raster layers

## Coordinate congruence

Census `PX, PY`, Wolf's soil `gx, gy` and elevation `x, y` use the same local plot coordinates, in metres. Here "x" increases eastward from the western edge and "y" increases northward from the southern edge. We use `"local"` as coordinate reference system (CRS) throughout. This will be enough for most standard applications in plot-based ecology. Check that any additional plot data share origin, axis directions and units.

External sources such as remote-sensing products need CRS alignment and standard GIS checks before use (`sf::st_transform()` or `terra::project()`, as appropriate). Remember that simply assigning a CRS label alone does not align coordinates!

## Terrain from the elevation grid

The example call uses default linear interpolation and selects a few of the variables available through `derive_topography()` fgeo2 function. Elevation is returned automatically too. This is an application of the completed [terrain workflow](derive-topographical-variables.qmd). TPI describes relative topographic position at the selected neighbourhood scale. Northness and eastness are relative to the local plot-grid axes here.

```{r}
#| label: prepare-terrain

head(xyz)

terrain <- derive_topography(
	xyz = xyz,
	variables = c("slope", "tpi", "northness", "eastness"),
	resolution = terrain.resolution,
	extent = plot.extent,
	crs = "local",
	position.radius = 20
)

names(terrain)
```

## Soil measurements to continuous layers

The soil coordinates are sampling locations. In the dataset we are using, they form an approximately 28 m sampling design with small positional offsets. For this tutorial example, inverse-distance weighting estimates P and Ca on a 20 m grid. Other example settings are: 60 m search radius, up to 12 neighbours, at least 3 observations and power 2. Visualize results to tune these parameters satisfactorily to your case. Note that the resulting cells describe interpolated estimates, not true measurement accuracy or uniform density of information. But this is standard practice, so in general you don't have to worry about this if data comes from a reasonable representative survey.

```{r}
#| label: prepare-soil

soil.template <- rast(xmin = 0, xmax = 1000, ymin = 0, ymax = 500,
                       resolution = soil.resolution, crs = "local")
soil.variables <- c("M3P", "M3Ca")
soil.layers <- vector("list", length(soil.variables))

for(i in seq_along(soil.variables))
{
	variable <- soil.variables[i]
	keep <- is.finite(soils$gx) & is.finite(soils$gy) & is.finite(soils[[variable]])
	
	measurements <- as.matrix(soils[keep, c("gx", "gy", variable)])
	soil.layers[[i]] <- interpIDW(soil.template, measurements,
	                              radius = 60, power = 2,
	                              minPoints = 3, maxPoints = 12)

	# Avoid extending these predictions beyond the sampling locations' hull.
	locations <- vect(soils[keep, ], geom = c("gx", "gy"), crs = "local")
	soil.layers[[i]] <- mask(soil.layers[[i]], convHull(locations), touches = FALSE)
}

soil <- rast(soil.layers)
names(soil) <- c("soil_P_mgkg", "soil_Ca_mgkg")
units(soil) <- c("mg/kg", "mg/kg")
```

For a table that already describes a complete regular grid of **cell centres**, conversion can be much shorter. Cell-centre positions and cell boundaries must be distinguished to avoid a half-cell shift.

```{r}
#| label: regular-table-template
#| eval: false

# Columns x and y are centres of cells in a known regular grid.
# Additional columns become separate raster layers.
regular.layers <- rast(my.table[c("x", "y", "soil_P", "soil_Ca")],
                        type = "xyz", crs = "local")
```

If environmental values are already recorded for the supplied quadrats, a direct ID join may be sufficient. Raster conversion is useful when the subsequent analysis actually needs a surface.

## Optional: use principal components

Many environmental datasets, including soil surveys, often contain many correlated variables, and could be described in terms of environmental (soil) axes. This optional example standardizes the soil measurement columns and fits PCA to complete rows. It excludes identifiers and coordinates, and preserves row alignment when storing scores.

```{r}
#| label: soil-pca
#| eval: false

coordinate.columns <- c("uid", "qid", "gx", "gy", "utm_e", "utm_n")
soil.columns <- setdiff(names(soils), c(coordinate.columns, "soil_PC1"))
keep <- complete.cases(soils[soil.columns])
soil.pca <- prcomp(soils[keep, soil.columns], center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)
soils$soil_PC1 <- NA_real_
soils$soil_PC1[keep] <- soil.pca$x[, 1]
summary(soil.pca)$importance[,1:5]

# To map PC1, apply the soil-interpolation block to soil_PC1.
# Retain soil.pca itself to inspect loadings and reproduce the scores.
```

# Combine sources and check their grids

## Retain native grids

A named list can hold the terrain and soil rasters together while preserving each grid. Sources with compatible grids can already be combined into a multilayer `SpatRaster`. Extraction below works through this list and joins the results by target identity.

```{r}
#| label: native-grids

environment <- list(terrain = terrain, soil = soil)

str(environment)
str(environment$terrain)
dim(environment$terrain)
str(environment$soil)
dim(environment$soil)

compareGeom(terrain, soil, stopOnError = FALSE)
```

Missing terrain neighbourhoods and the soil sampling hull create different valid footprints, even though both raster extents describe the full plot. An optional check below shows how much of a target contributes valid values when this matters to an analysis.

## Create a common grid when needed

For cell-wise calculations, use one chosen template. Here both sources have the same extent, origin and CRS, and 20 m is an integer multiple of 5 m. Aggregating groups of 4 × 4 terrain cells produces a compatible grid. With compatible grids, adding variables is simply `c()`.

```{r}
#| label: common-grid

terrain20 <- aggregate(terrain, fact = 4, fun = "mean", na.rm = TRUE)
stopifnot(compareGeom(terrain20, soil))
common.grid <- c(terrain20, soil)
names(common.grid)
```

These are means of the fine-resolution terrain variables. Calculating slope or TPI afresh from a coarser DEM would define a different quantity. `na.rm = TRUE` also permits partially observed aggregate cells. Extraction below uses the native layers in `environment`.

For other situations, choose the operation according to the actual mismatch.

| Situation                                  | Operation and interpretation                                                                        |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| Same grid, additional variables            | `c()` adds layers after `compareGeom()` checks.                                                     |
| Aligned fine cells to larger cells         | `aggregate()` summarizes groups of cells.                                                           |
| Same CRS, different grid origin or spacing | `resample()` transfers values to an explicit template. Choose a method appropriate to the variable. |
| Adjacent tiles of one variable             | `merge()` or `mosaic()` combines spatial tiles.                                                     |

For continuous point-like surfaces, bilinear resampling is a possible interpolation choice. For larger output cells covering several input cells, a mean may be appropriate. A value representing a block mean has a different meaning from a measurement at its centre. Smoothing changes the environmental surface and should have a stated analytical purpose. Finer output cells retain the information limits of the original source.

```{r}
#| label: resampling-template
#| eval: false

# Same known CRS, but grids that do not align.
soil.on.terrain.grid <- resample(soil, terrain[[1]], method = "bilinear")
# A coarser output template may instead call for method = "mean".
```

# Extract at point (tree) coordinates

This example uses three tree species. The extraction itself works on points: it has no species-specific requirements and can be applied to all supplied records.

```{r}
#| label: choose-tree-targets
spp <- c("beilpe", "virosu", "elaeol")
use <- which(trees$Mnemonic %in% spp & trees$Status == "alive")
targets <- trees[use, c("point_id", "Census", "StemID", "Mnemonic", "PX", "PY")]

rownames(targets) <- NULL
table(targets$Census, targets$Mnemonic)
```

The `terra::extract()` function crosses layers with sampling points; `method = "simple"` returns the value of the cell containing each point. Optional bilinear sampling estimates a value from nearby cell centres and changes the sampling operation.

Keep the identifiers and census columns in `targets`, and append the extracted values. Terra returns one row per point in the supplied order, including repeated coordinates and points with missing or outside locations. `ID = FALSE` omits terra's additional row-number column.

```{r}
#| label: sample-points

points <- vect(targets, geom = c("PX", "PY"), crs = "local")
point.env <- targets
for(layers in environment)
	point.env <- cbind(point.env,
	                   terra::extract(layers, points, method = "simple", ID = FALSE))

head(point.env[c("point_id", "Mnemonic", "elevation_m", "soil_P_mgkg")])

# Group the extracted values by species.
aggregate(point.env[c("elevation_m", "soil_P_mgkg", "soil_Ca_mgkg")],
          by = list(point.env$Mnemonic), FUN = mean, na.rm = TRUE)
```

# Extract from buffers

**Note: All polygon-based extractions work in the same way.** The tutorial separates buffers, quadrats and arbitrary polygons for didactic purposes, and is clearly repetitive: only the target construction changes. Package `terra` is sufficient for means. Package `exactextractr` conveniently supplies several overlap-weighted statistics and valid-area totals together.

## Construct buffers

The radius is in metres. Buffers may overlap and cross the plot boundary. Missing point coordinates become empty buffer geometries. Keep their original rows, and use `buffer.i` to select the defined geometries for exactextractr.

```{r}
#| label: point-buffers

buffers <- st_buffer(st_as_sf(points), dist = buffer.radius)
buffer.i <- which(!st_is_empty(buffers))
if(!length(buffer.i)) stop("No buffers have a usable location.")
```

## Extract environmental summaries

Each package summarizes all polygons and raster layers in one call. The loop only visits sources whose native grids differ. Results follow the input geometry order, so `cbind()` retains the original identifiers and attributes.

### Method 1 with terra::extract()

`exact = TRUE` weights polygon means by partial-cell overlaps; `na.rm = TRUE` omits missing cell values. The output columns retain the raster variable names.

```{r}
#| label: terra-buffer-means

buffer.terra <- targets
for(layers in environment)
{
	means <- terra::extract(layers, vect(buffers), fun = mean,
	                        exact = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE, ID = FALSE)
	buffer.terra <- cbind(buffer.terra, means)
}
```

### Method 2 with exactextractr::exact_extract()

Named summaries such as `"mean"`, `"median"` and `"stdev"` already account for overlap weights and omit missing values. Edit the `fun` vector to choose summaries. `force_df = TRUE` keeps a dataframe result even when selecting only one variable and summary.

Indexed subsetting restores rows omitted because their buffer geometry was empty. The examples require at least one non-empty polygon.

```{r}
#| label: exactextractr-buffer-summaries

buffer.env <- targets
for(layers in environment)
{
	extracted <- exact_extract(layers, buffers[buffer.i, ],
		fun = c("mean", "median", "stdev"),
		full_colnames = TRUE, force_df = TRUE, progress = FALSE)

	extracted <- extracted[match(seq_len(nrow(targets)), buffer.i), , drop = FALSE]
	buffer.env <- cbind(buffer.env, extracted)
}
```

Both methods retain undefined estimates as `NA` or `NaN`; `is.na()` identifies either. An area without valid raster values and an unresolved location both lack an environmental estimate. These conventions also apply to quadrats and arbitrary polygons below.

`stdev` is the overlap-weighted population SD: spatial heterogeneity within the area. Estimating uncertainty in a surface or its mean needs information about measurement or model error; raster cells should not automatically be treated as independent observations for a standard error.

## Check the buffer results

`buffer.env` retains one row per tree/stem record, including its original identifiers.

```{r}
#| label: check-buffer-results

head(buffer.env[c("point_id", "mean.soil_P_mgkg",
                  "median.soil_P_mgkg", "stdev.soil_P_mgkg")])
```

# Extract from quadrats

## Construct quadrats

Reuse `make_quadrats_fast()` and the standard table with `quadrat_id`, `xmin`, `ymin`, `xmax` and `ymax`. Set `RESOLUTION` to the quadrat side length in metres, then rerun this section to explore other sizes, such as 50 m. The polygons come directly from the bounds.

```{r}
#| label: quadrat-polygons

RESOLUTION = 20 # Change this to extract for quadrats of a different size (m).
quadrat.table <- make_quadrats_fast(0, 0, 1000, 500, RESOLUTION, RESOLUTION)

geometry <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(quadrat.table)), function(i)
{
	q <- quadrat.table[i, ]
	corners <- cbind(c(q$xmin, q$xmax, q$xmax, q$xmin, q$xmin),
	                 c(q$ymin, q$ymin, q$ymax, q$ymax, q$ymin))
	st_polygon(list(corners))
})

quadrats <- st_sf(quadrat.table, geometry = st_sfc(geometry, crs = st_crs(crs(terrain))))
```

## Extract environmental summaries

The recipes are the same as for buffers. The environmental rasters retain their native resolution at any quadrat size.

### Method 1 with terra::extract()

```{r}
#| label: terra-quadrat-means

quadrat.terra <- quadrat.table
for(layers in environment)
{
	means <- terra::extract(layers, vect(quadrats), fun = mean,
	                        exact = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE, ID = FALSE)
	quadrat.terra <- cbind(quadrat.terra, means)
}
```

### Method 2 with exactextractr::exact_extract()

```{r}
#| label: exactextractr-quadrat-summaries

quadrat.env <- quadrat.table
for(layers in environment)
{
	extracted <- exact_extract(layers, quadrats,
		fun = c("mean", "median", "stdev"),
		full_colnames = TRUE, force_df = TRUE, progress = FALSE)

	quadrat.env <- cbind(quadrat.env, extracted)
}
```

## Check the quadrat results

The output retains each quadrat's bounds and ID.

```{r}
#| label: check-quadrat-results

head(quadrat.env[c("quadrat_id", "mean.soil_P_mgkg", "stdev.soil_P_mgkg")])
```

# Extract from arbitrary polygons

## Construct the polygons

In this example, one polygon lies inside the plot and the other crosses its western boundary. Existing `sf` polygons or multipolygons in the same local frame can enter here. Correct invalid shapes before extraction. If some locations are unresolved, `polygon.i` selects non-empty geometries while their original output rows remain available.

```{r}
#| label: irregular-polygons

regions <- st_sf(polygon_id = c("interior", "western_edge"),
	geometry = st_sfc(
		st_polygon(list(cbind(c(100, 240, 190, 100), c(150, 150, 280, 150)))),
		st_polygon(list(cbind(c(-15, 60, 60, -15, -15), c(30, 30, 80, 100, 30)))),
		crs = st_crs(crs(terrain))
	))

polygon.table <- st_drop_geometry(regions)
polygon.i <- which(!st_is_empty(regions))
stopifnot(all(st_is_valid(regions)))
if(!length(polygon.i)) stop("Supply at least one non-empty polygon.")
```

## Extract environmental summaries

Only the target geometry has changed. Summaries use the available raster values within each polygon.

### Method 1 with terra::extract()

```{r}
#| label: terra-polygon-means

polygon.terra <- polygon.table
for(layers in environment)
{
	means <- terra::extract(layers, vect(regions), fun = mean,
	                        exact = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE, ID = FALSE)
	polygon.terra <- cbind(polygon.terra, means)
}
```

### Method 2 with exactextractr::exact_extract()

```{r}
#| label: exactextractr-polygon-summaries

polygon.env <- polygon.table
for(layers in environment)
{
	extracted <- exact_extract(layers, regions[polygon.i, ],
		fun = c("mean", "median", "stdev"),
		full_colnames = TRUE, force_df = TRUE, progress = FALSE)

  extracted <- extracted[match(seq_len(nrow(polygon.table)), polygon.i), , drop = FALSE]
	polygon.env <- cbind(polygon.env, extracted)
}
```

## Check the polygon results

The western-edge polygon still receives summaries, using its overlap with valid cells. Soil and terrain can have different valid footprints.

```{r}
#| label: check-polygon-results

polygon.env[c("polygon_id", "mean.elevation_m", "mean.soil_P_mgkg")]
```

## Optional check: valid environmental area

For targets crossing a raster boundary or containing missing cells, valid-area coverage can flag a mean based on only a small part of the intended area. It is useful for deciding whether to retain such targets, but need not accompany every extraction. Coverage measures available raster area, not measurement accuracy or interpolation uncertainty.

Here `"count"` with `coverage_area = TRUE` returns the area with non-missing soil P values, in square metres. Dividing by the full polygon area gives its valid fraction: 0.7 would mean that 70% of the target contributes to the summary. This check is specific to the selected variable.

```{r}
#| label: optional-valid-area

valid.area <- exact_extract(soil[["soil_P_mgkg"]], regions[polygon.i, ],
	fun = "count", coverage_area = TRUE, progress = FALSE)
coverage <- polygon.table
coverage$valid_fraction <- NA_real_
coverage$valid_fraction[polygon.i] <-
	valid.area / as.numeric(st_area(regions[polygon.i, ]))
coverage
```

# Pseudo-legacy for quadrat-level topography

This example uses the same BCI elevation table to compare original CTFS/fgeo calculations with a compact raster route at 20 m quadrat resolution.

## Original CTFS calculation

Use the repository's snapshot loader to download the archived original scripts from a fixed commit, keeping their functions in a separate environment. The original calculation expects a table named `col`, an elevation column named `elev`, and grid locations ordered by x, then y. The BCI table supplies the required quadrat corners and perimeter midpoints for `edgecorrect = TRUE`.

```{r}
#| label: legacy-quadrat-topography
#| results: hide
#| message: false

source(file.path(path.to.fgeo2, "evaluation/0-code-to-source.r"))
legacy <- new.env()
load_github_snapshot(
	commit = "0a2c01dd560daacba0fdc2eb8c9280e2b9d2ea9d",
	scripts = c("evaluation/Condit/spatial/quadfunc.r",
	            "evaluation/Condit/topography/slope.r"),
	envir = legacy
)

legacy.xyz <- xyz[order(xyz$x, xyz$y), ]
names(legacy.xyz)[names(legacy.xyz) == "z"] <- "elev"

legacy.topography <- legacy$allquadratslopes(
	list(col = legacy.xyz), gridsize = 20,
	plotdim = c(1000, 500), edgecorrect = TRUE
)
```

## Alternative fgeo2 calculation at a comparable scale

Use 5 m cells, a 3 × 3 cell smoothing window (15 × 15 m), and `position.radius = 25` for TPI. The latter defines an 11 × 11 cell window covering 55 × 55 m, broadly comparable to the three-by-three set of 20 m quadrats used for interior legacy convexity. These are useful scale choices for this example, rather than a guarantee for other surfaces.

Because the 20 m quadrats align with groups of 4 × 4 raster cells, aggregation followed by sampling at quadrat centres gives means over their available raster area. This is a short alternative to constructing polygons for this aligned grid. It summarizes the derived terrain layers; it does not calculate slope from a 20 m DEM.

```{r}
#| label: raster-quadrat-topography

q <- make_quadrats_fast(0, 0, 1000, 500, 20, 20)

quadrat.terrain <- derive_topography(
	xyz = xyz, variables = c("slope", "tpi"),
	resolution = 5, extent = plot.extent, crs = "local",
	smoothing.cells = 3, position.radius = 25
)

topography20 <- aggregate(quadrat.terrain, fact = 4, fun = "mean", na.rm = TRUE)
quadrat.xy <- cbind(x = (q$xmin + q$xmax) / 2,
	                y = (q$ymin + q$ymax) / 2)

raster.topography <- cbind(q, terra::extract(topography20, quadrat.xy))
```

## Compare old and new approaches

First check row alignment against the original quadrat indexing. Compare quadrats at least 40 m inside the plot boundary so all fine cells have complete terrain neighbourhoods. This also avoids the different edge rule in legacy convexity.

```{r}
#| label: compare-quadrat-topography

legacy.xy <- legacy$index.to.gxgy(seq_len(nrow(legacy.topography)),
	gridsize = 20, plotdim = c(1000, 500))
stopifnot(all(legacy.xy$gx == q$xmin), all(legacy.xy$gy == q$ymin))

interior <- q$xmin >= 40 & q$xmax <= 960 & q$ymin >= 40 & q$ymax <= 460
legacy.values <- legacy.topography[interior, c("meanelev", "slope", "convex")]
raster.values <- raster.topography[interior, c("elevation_m", "slope_deg", "tpi_m")]

comparison <- data.frame(
	variable = c("Elevation (m)", "Slope (degrees)", "Convexity / TPI (m)"),
	quadrats = nrow(legacy.values),
	correlation = diag(cor(legacy.values, raster.values)),
	mean.absolute.difference = colMeans(abs(raster.values - legacy.values))
)

knitr::kable(comparison, row.names = FALSE, digits = c(0, 0, 4, 3),
	col.names = c("Variable", "Quadrats", "Correlation", "Mean absolute difference"))
```

For these 966 interior quadrats, mean absolute differences are about 0.074 m for elevation, 0.252 degrees for slope and 0.060 m for TPI versus convexity. Both routes capture similar broad topographic gradients. The original method uses quadrat-corner elevations and plane slopes, whereas the raster route summarizes cell values and local derivatives. TPI remains a different measure from legacy convexity, so identical thresholds or habitat assignments should not be assumed. This comparison measures agreement on one input surface, not independent terrain accuracy.

# Save results and reuse them

Save native raster groups separately to retain their original resolution. GeoTIFF files can be loaded directly with `rast()` in later work. The common-grid object can be saved as an additional explicit product if needed. Tabular outputs remain separate from geometry and can feed later habitat analyses or mapping workflows.

```{r}
#| label: save-environment
#| results: hide

writeRaster(terrain, file.path(output.dir, "bci-terrain.tif"), overwrite = TRUE)
writeRaster(soil, file.path(output.dir, "bci-soil.tif"), overwrite = TRUE)
write.csv(point.env, file.path(output.dir, "bci-point-environment.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(buffer.env, file.path(output.dir, "bci-buffer-environment.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(quadrat.env, file.path(output.dir, "bci-quadrat-environment.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(polygon.env, file.path(output.dir, "bci-polygon-environment.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

# Independent raster inputs in a later session.
saved.soil <- rast(file.path(output.dir, "bci-soil.tif"))
stopifnot(compareGeom(saved.soil, soil))
```

Keep the original inputs, source licences, parameter choices and executed code with the analysis. The examples above use the same target rows for each variable, while the valid observations contributing to each summary can differ. Any subsequent filtering should be explicit in that analysis.

# Software references and versions

-   [terra extraction](https://rspatial.github.io/terra/reference/extract.html) and [point interpolation](https://rspatial.github.io/terra/reference/interpIDW.html).
-   [terra grid comparisons](https://rspatial.github.io/terra/reference/compareGeom.html), [aggregation](https://rspatial.github.io/terra/reference/aggregate.html) and [resampling](https://rspatial.github.io/terra/reference/resample.html).
-   [exactextractr summaries and custom functions](https://isciences.gitlab.io/exactextractr/reference/exact_extract.html).
-   [sf coordinate transformations](https://r-spatial.github.io/sf/reference/st_transform.html).

```{r}
#| label: environment-session

packages <- c("terra", "sf", "interp", "exactextractr")
data.frame(software = c("R", packages),
           version = c(as.character(getRversion()),
                       sapply(packages, function(x) as.character(packageVersion(x)))))
# sessionInfo() gives a full session record for an analysis archive.
```
